levels.title: Computers & the Internet in One Level
levels.objective: After this level you can follow a single photo from your phone's switches and software, across the internet, to a friend's screen.

levels.title: A Bit: The Smallest Fact
levels.objective: After this level you can explain a bit as one yes-or-no choice and why eight bits make a byte with 256 possible patterns.

levels.title: Kilobytes to Terabytes
levels.objective: After this level you can compare the sizes of a text message, a photo, a movie and a whole drive in bytes.

levels.title: How Letters Become Numbers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how codes like ASCII and Unicode give every letter, symbol and emoji its own number.

levels.title: Pictures and Sound as Numbers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a photo becomes a grid of pixel numbers and a song becomes thousands of samples a second.

levels.title: Logic Gates: AND, OR, NOT
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how AND, OR and NOT gates turn yes-or-no inputs into a yes-or-no output.

levels.title: Adding With Switches
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a handful of logic gates can add two binary numbers, the first step toward all computing.

levels.title: The Processor's Endless Loop
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the fetch, decode and execute cycle a processor repeats billions of times a second.

levels.title: Why Memory Comes in Layers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a computer keeps data in layers, from tiny fast cache to roomy RAM to big slow storage.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Inside the Machine
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how bits, gates, a processor and memory turn stored numbers into text, pictures and sums.

levels.title: Punched Cards
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how punched cards steered a weaving loom in 1804 and counted the 1890 US census.

levels.title: Ada Lovelace's Big Idea
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Lovelace's 1843 insight that Babbage's Analytical Engine could work with symbols, not just numbers.

levels.title: Turing's Imaginary Machine
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Alan Turing's 1936 idea of a simple machine reading a tape, and why it can compute anything computable.

levels.title: ENIAC and Its Programmers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how ENIAC was programmed by rewiring cables and switches, and who did that work.

levels.title: Keeping the Program in Memory
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why storing the program in memory beside its data, first done in 1948, made computers flexible.

levels.title: The Transistor
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the 1947 transistor replaced hot, fragile vacuum tubes as the computer's switch.

levels.title: Chips and Moore's Law
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the integrated circuit and Gordon Moore's 1965 prediction that the parts on a chip would keep doubling.

levels.title: The Computer Comes Home
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the cheap microprocessor led to the Altair, the Apple II and the IBM PC, and put computers in homes.

levels.title: The Smartphone Era
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the smartphone and its app stores, from 2007 on, became most people's main computer.

levels.title: Checkpoint: How Computers Came to Be
levels.objective: After this level you can trace computing from punched cards to smartphones and name the switch that powered each era.

levels.title: Spell Out Every Step
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a program must spell out every step exactly, because a computer never fills in what you meant.

levels.title: From Code to Machine Code
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how compilers and interpreters turn code people can read into instructions a processor runs.

levels.title: Why So Many Languages?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why languages like Python, JavaScript and C all exist, each suited to different jobs.

levels.title: Remember, Choose, Repeat
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the three moves nearly every program makes: storing values in variables, choosing with if, and repeating with loops.

levels.title: Binary Search: Halve and Halve Again
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how binary search finds one name in a sorted list of a million in about 20 steps.

levels.title: Why Some Recipes Scale Badly
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the steps an algorithm needs grow as its input grows, and why that decides whether it is usable.

levels.title: One Processor, Many Programs
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the operating system switches the processor between programs so quickly they seem to run at once.

levels.title: Where Deleted Files Go
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a file system tracks where files live, and why a "deleted" file can often be recovered.

levels.title: Bugs
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a bug creeps into a program, from the 1947 moth to the 1996 Ariane 5 rocket failure.

levels.title: Checkpoint: How Software Works
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a program is written, translated, run and shared out by the operating system, and how it goes wrong.

levels.title: What a Network Is
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a home or office network links devices through a switch or router so they can share data.

levels.title: IP Addresses
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how every device online gets an IP address, and why IPv4's 4.3 billion addresses ran out.

levels.title: DNS: The Internet's Phone Book
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how DNS turns a name like example.com into the number address a computer can reach.

levels.title: Routers Pass It On
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how routers forward each packet one hop at a time, with no single machine knowing the whole route.

levels.title: Lost Packets and Second Tries
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how TCP numbers packets, checks that all of them arrived and asks again for missing ones.

levels.title: Layers: Envelopes in Envelopes
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how internet protocols wrap data in layers, each layer doing one job for the one above.

levels.title: Light in Glass: Fiber Optics
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how fiber optic cables carry data as pulses of light kept inside thin strands of glass.

levels.title: One Address, Many Devices
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how your home router shares one public address among all your devices.

levels.title: The Last Mile
levels.objective: After this level you can compare how homes connect to the internet by cable, fiber, cell networks and low-orbit satellites.

levels.title: Checkpoint: How the Internet Works
levels.objective: After this level you can trace a packet from your device through addresses, DNS, routers and cables and explain how it arrives complete.

levels.title: Asking for a Page
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the request and response behind every web page, and why the web was built to forget you between requests.

levels.title: Pages Built From Instructions
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a web page arrives as HTML, CSS and JavaScript that your browser assembles into what you see.

levels.title: Cookies
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why websites use cookies to remember you, and how third-party cookies follow you across sites.

levels.title: Why the Cloud Won
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why companies rent computing from cloud providers instead of running their own servers, and what they give up.

levels.title: Inside a Data Center
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why data centers need so much electricity and cooling, and why that shapes where they are built.

levels.title: Why Fast Internet Still Lags
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the difference between bandwidth and latency, and why distance adds a delay no faster plan removes.

levels.title: Copies Near You
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why popular videos and pages are copied to servers close to viewers, and what that saves.

levels.title: Squeezing Data: Compression
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why photos and video can shrink to a fraction of their size, and what lossy compression throws away.

levels.title: Why Websites Go Down
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why outages happen and how one small change can spread, using the 2021 Facebook outage.

levels.title: Milestone: One Web Page, Start to Finish
levels.objective: After this level you can explain every step from typing a web address to seeing the page: bits, software, DNS, packets, servers and your browser.

levels.title: Why Updates Matter
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why all complex software has security holes, what a zero-day is, and why installing updates quickly matters.

levels.title: How Sites Store Passwords
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a well-run site keeps only a scrambled hash of your password, never the password itself.

levels.title: Why Long Passwords Win
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why each extra character multiplies an attacker's guesses, and why one reused password unlocks many accounts.

levels.title: Two-Factor and Passkeys
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a second factor, or a passkey that never leaves your device, stops most stolen-password attacks.

levels.title: Public Keys: The Open Padlock
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how public-key cryptography lets two strangers agree on a secret over a line anyone can hear.

levels.title: The Padlock in Your Browser
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why HTTPS certificates prove you reached the real site, and what the browser padlock does not promise.

levels.title: Viruses, Worms and Trojans
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how viruses, worms and trojans differ in the way they get onto a computer and spread.

levels.title: Ransomware
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why ransomware attacks hospitals, cities and companies, and why backups are the best defense.

levels.title: Phishing: Hacking the Human
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why phishing works by rushing and tricking people rather than breaking code, and spot its signs.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Security Online
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why attackers target people, passwords and old software, and which defenses stop each kind of attack.

levels.title: What a Database Is
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a database stores records in tables and uses an index to find one among billions.

levels.title: The Data Your Phone Gives Off
levels.objective: After this level you can connect cookies, apps and location settings to the data trail your phone leaves in a normal day.

levels.title: Metadata: The Envelope
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why who, when and where you communicate can reveal as much as what you said.

levels.title: Why "Free" Apps Show Ads
levels.objective: After this level you can connect the ad-funded business model to the data that apps and websites collect about you.

levels.title: Data Brokers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how companies you have never dealt with buy, combine and sell profiles of people.

levels.title: Anonymous Data That Isn't
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how combining a few details, like ZIP code, birth date and sex, can put a name back on "anonymous" data.

levels.title: Data Breaches
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what happens in a data breach, using Equifax in 2017, and connect it to the hashing and two-factor defenses.

levels.title: End-to-End Encryption
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why end-to-end encryption means even the service can't read your messages, and why governments debate it.

levels.title: Privacy Laws
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what laws like the EU's GDPR and California's privacy law let you ask of companies that hold your data.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Your Data and Privacy
levels.objective: After this level you can trace where your personal data goes, who profits from it, and which laws and tools limit what happens to it.

levels.title: How Maps Find the Fastest Route
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a route-finding algorithm explores a road network step by step and uses live traffic to update it.

levels.title: "Because You Watched"
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how recommendation systems suggest things by finding people whose tastes match yours.

levels.title: How Your Feed Is Ranked
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how social feeds score posts by predicted engagement instead of showing them in time order.

levels.title: The Auction Behind Every Ad
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how an ad space is auctioned in a fraction of a second while a page loads, using data about you.

levels.title: How Spam Filters Learn
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a spam filter learns from labeled examples which words and signals predict junk mail.

levels.title: Matching Riders and Drivers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how ride and delivery apps match each request to a nearby driver and raise prices when demand spikes.

levels.title: Moderating Billions of Posts
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how platforms combine automated filters and human reviewers, and why both make mistakes at scale.

levels.title: Feedback Loops
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a recommendation can shape the very behavior it later learns from.

levels.title: Who Checks the Algorithm?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how audits, explanations and appeal rights let people test and challenge automated decisions.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Algorithms That Choose
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how routes, recommendations, feeds, ads and filters are chosen for you, and who can check them.

levels.title: Rules or Examples?
levels.objective: After this level you can decide whether a task is better solved by writing rules or by learning from examples, and say why.

levels.title: Training and Testing
levels.objective: After this level you can judge a model by how it does on data it never saw, and spot overfitting when it only memorized its training set.

levels.title: Inside a Neural Network
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a neural network learns by nudging millions of weights, a little at a time, to shrink its errors.

levels.title: Why AI Needs So Many Chips
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why training large models takes thousands of graphics chips and large amounts of electricity.

levels.title: Tokens and the Next Word
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a large language model splits text into tokens and writes by predicting one token after another.

levels.title: From Predictor to Assistant
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how pretraining on vast amounts of text, then fine-tuning with human feedback, turns a text predictor into a chatbot.

levels.title: Why Chatbots Make Things Up
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a language model can state false things fluently, and check a chatbot's answer against a source.

levels.title: Pictures From Noise
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how image generators learn to turn random noise, step by step, into a picture that matches a prompt.

levels.title: Deepfakes and Proving What's Real
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh the ways to tell a real photo, video or voice from a synthetic one, including provenance labels.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Machine Learning and AI
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how machine learning, neural networks and language models learn from data, and where each one fails.

levels.title: Megabits, Megabytes and Speed
levels.objective: After this level you can work out a real download time from an advertised internet speed, and spot claims that mix up bits and bytes.

levels.title: Is My Phone Listening to Me?
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh the evidence on whether phones secretly record conversations for ads, and the simpler explanations for eerie ads.

levels.title: What AI Can and Can't Do in 2026
levels.objective: After this level you can judge a claim about AI against what current systems reliably do and where they still fail.

levels.title: Will Quantum Break Encryption?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain which kinds of encryption a large quantum computer could break, and how post-quantum standards prepare for it.

levels.title: Hype and the Dot-Com Bubble
levels.objective: After this level you can judge a new technology's hype using the rise and crash of internet stocks around 2000 as a guide.

levels.title: Is Moore's Law Over?
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh the arguments over whether chip progress is slowing, and what engineers do now that shrinking is harder.

levels.title: Open or Closed Software?
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh the trade-offs between open-source and closed software for security, cost and control.

levels.title: The Internet's Energy Bill
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh estimates of how much electricity data centers use and what is driving the growth.

levels.title: Your Checklist for Tech Claims
levels.objective: After this level you can run any claim about a gadget, app or AI through a short set of questions: how it works, who says so, and what it costs you.

levels.title: Mastery Challenge: Computers & the Internet
levels.objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Computers & the Internet Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
